title: The monarch’s quiet role: advice, reserve powers and why secrecy matters
label: 16 September 2026 · The UK’s constitutional safeguards
summary: Former royal private secretary Lord Young explains how the monarch works behind the scenes: a private weekly meeting with the Prime Minister where the sovereign is 'consulted, encourages and warns', and how that confidentiality helps prevent crises. He describes rare situations where the monarch might use reserve powers, stresses limits on intervention when Parliament acts democratically, and urges better education and an updated Cabinet Manual to strengthen practical safeguards.

speakers.label: Lord Young of Old Windsor
speakers.name: Lord Young of Old Windsor
speakers.role: former principal private secretary to the sovereign

chapters.title: The weekly audience and how the monarchy actually works
chapters.takeaway: The monarch meets the Prime Minister privately each week to be 'consulted, to encourage and to warn' — a practice that keeps government steady.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Young, welcome. To start: how would you describe the monarch’s role in today’s government?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Thanks. From working in the Royal Household nearly 20 years, the core is the weekly private audience between the monarch and the Prime Minister — usually an hour after PMQs.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Before the meeting the Prime Minister talks briefly with the private secretary. The private secretary and I then meet the Prime Minister’s private secretary downstairs. We call it keeping a link between Head of State and Head of Government.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: That hour matters. The PM can speak freely, won’t get quoted on social media, and hears a long-term, non-partisan perspective. It steadies leaders and reduces rash moves.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: So it’s practical, not ceremonial — it has real day-to-day impact?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Exactly. It’s practical and confidential. The sovereign’s role in that meeting is to be consulted, to encourage and to warn — not to campaign or take sides.

chapters.title: Why confidentiality is vital — and how it sits with public trust
chapters.takeaway: Private conversations let leaders be candid; the monarchy builds public trust by acting consistently and representing long-term national interests.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You stress privacy. Is that really essential?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Absolutely. If those talks were public, ministers couldn’t speak candidly. The Freedom of Information idea of protecting 'formulation of policy' helps — draft thinking needs protection.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: But people want transparency. How do you build trust if the public can’t see these talks?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It’s a paradox. You build trust by other visible acts: steady constitutional behaviour, representing the nation, meeting many communities over years. Consistent, non-partisan action over time reassures people.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: So visibility in public-facing roles balances confidentiality behind closed doors?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. The monarchy’s long-term perspective — thinking years ahead rather than today’s headlines — helps bridge that trust gap.

chapters.title: When the monarch might act beyond advice — reserve powers
chapters.takeaway: There are rare reserve powers the monarch could use in a crisis, for example if there’s uncertainty about who should be Prime Minister or an abuse like asking to prorogue Parliament to avoid losing power.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Could the monarch ever act as a stronger restraint — more than just giving warnings?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, in theory. The constitution isn’t all written down; many parts are customs tested over time. Reserve powers exist, for instance over appointing a Prime Minister if it’s unclear who can command the House.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Another example: the sovereign might refuse a request to prorogue (suspend) Parliament if it was being used to avoid losing power. But those are extreme, last‑resort steps.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: Imagine a Government loses a confidence vote but refuses to resign — deadlock. What then?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It depends on personalities and how rotten the situation is. If the Government truly had no support and the Cabinet collapsed, the sovereign might have to act. But often the system — Cabinet, Parliament, courts — would sort it first.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: Is ambiguity about these powers useful because it lets the system adapt?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I think so. A rigid written rule can’t predict every crisis. The ambiguity allows experienced advisers to work things out in real time — but it relies on people acting in good faith.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: You gave an example about Boris Johnson and Covid — what happened there?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: When the PM was seriously ill, we had no clear precedent for an in‑office, temporarily incapacitated Prime Minister in a crisis. Officials worked out a temporary plan: the Cabinet Secretary would convene Cabinet to recommend who to appoint briefly if needed. It was ad hoc but effective.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: Some point to Australia’s 1975 dismissal of Gough Whitlam. Could that happen here?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Whitlam is a cautionary tale. The present Australian Governor‑General has said she can’t imagine repeating that now. In the UK, I find it hard to see it happening unless the whole government machinery collapsed — unpaid staff, no functioning Cabinet.

chapters.title: Limits of royal intervention and the role of advisers
chapters.takeaway: The monarch can’t easily overturn laws a democratically elected Parliament has passed; private secretaries and other officials act as constitutional guardians.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Suppose a Government legally imposes press censorship — where does the monarchy stand?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If a democratically elected government passed such laws after winning an election on that platform, it would be very difficult for the sovereign to stop it. The monarchy isn’t a super‑parliamentary power in those circumstances.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Is the private secretary to the monarch a guardian of the constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. That post is one of several constitutional guardians. Private secretaries, the Cabinet Secretary, senior civil servants and judges all help protect constitutional norms.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Has that guardianship changed over time?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Not really. Predecessors I spoke to from the 1950s onwards followed similar principles: try to anticipate problems and prevent crises before they become public.

chapters.title: Practical safeguards and what could be improved
chapters.takeaway: The system is resilient but not perfect: keep vigilance, update the Cabinet Manual, and teach people earlier about how the constitution actually works.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you think our constitutional safeguards are sufficient?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I don’t want to sound complacent. From my experience, I see no clearly better system than ours, but it depends on people acting in good faith. We should stay vigilant.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Two practical steps: update the Cabinet Manual so it reflects recent practice, and improve education so people understand our uncodified constitution earlier in life.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: If a determined Government controls Parliament, are any safeguards left?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If a majority Government legitimately passes laws, it’s hard to see constitutional bodies overturning that. The trouble is when democratic outcome and public perception diverge because of electoral quirks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Lord Young. Any final point?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Only that the system’s strengths are the human relationships, the careful, confidential advice and shared practices. Keep those strong, teach the basics, and refresh guidance documents like the Cabinet Manual.
